1	\section{Introduction}
2	
3	Execution traces (line-by-line records of a program's runtime behavior) have emerged as a promising input modality for code language models \citep{chen2025tracepile,ding2024traced,wang2025dcsh,ni2024next}.
4	Yet feeding thousands of trace lines to a model can be no better than feeding none: the diagnostic signal drowns in routine execution steps.
5	\emph{Which trace components actually carry the signal that matters?}
6	
7	Prior work found no single trace representation consistently outperforms others \citep{wang2025dcsh}, but focused on generation-oriented tasks.
8	\emph{Verdict prediction}---classifying whether a test passes or fails---offers a cleaner testbed: as binary classification, it isolates the learning signal from generation noise, enabling controlled component ablation.
9	As fault detection, the model need not simulate execution, only determine whether something went wrong---and if that signal is concentrated in a small trace subset, information density should matter more than quantity.
10	
11	We test this hypothesis through the first systematic component ablation of trace representations for verdict prediction.
12	Using 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program}, we decompose a multi-component trace representation (VOTA: exception events + assertion-point comparisons + loop compression) into individual components across four models spanning 1.5B to 13B parameters and three architecture families: Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B/1.5B-Instruct \citep{qwen2025coder}, CodeLlama-13B-Instruct \citep{roziere2024code}, and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct \citep{deepseek2024coder}.
13	The results are striking: complete traces (${\sim}$80\%) underperform a single compact component (${\geq}$99\%) despite containing strictly more information---a direct demonstration that information density, not quantity, determines learning efficiency.
14	
15	\textbf{Exception events alone achieve ${\geq}$99.33\% verdict accuracy across all four models and all seeds tested} (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).
16	This near-perfect accuracy holds from 1.5B to 13B parameters, while the code-only baseline (\texttt{no\_trace}) varies from 67.3\% to 76.5\% with strong scale dependence.
17	Training dynamics confirm the density hypothesis: high-density inputs converge rapidly and stably, while verbose traces oscillate without reaching stable accuracy even when gradient dilution is eliminated (Figure~\ref{fig:training_dynamics}).
18	
19	Adding trace information beyond exceptions provides no benefit: VOTA (${\geq}$98.57\% across all models, excluding outlier seeds) slightly underperforms \texttt{exception\_only} on Qwen-7B (99.05\% vs.\ 99.83\%), with both conditions achieving near-ceiling accuracy across architectures.
20	The performance gap approximately decomposes into information overload (${\sim}$76\%) and gradient dilution (${\sim}$24\%) on Qwen-7B (3 seeds).
21	A tail-truncation budget sweep across four models reveals a phase transition at ${\sim}$500 tokens, with \texttt{tail\_2048} recovering 95--98\% of \texttt{exception\_only}'s accuracy.
22	Even on silent logic errors (55.5\% of failures), \texttt{exception\_only} maintains 100\% recall because test assertions generate exception events.
23	
24	Our contributions:
25	\begin{enumerate}
26	\item \textbf{Information density determines SFT learning efficiency}: training dynamics directly show that denser trace components learn faster and more stably---\texttt{exception\_only} converges within 50 steps while \texttt{full\_trace} with label-only loss oscillates (82--89\%) without stable convergence. Seed variance negatively correlates with input density ($\sigma{=}$0.00 to 1.12), and SFT closes a 6--49pp zero-shot gap across all models (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics}).
27	\item \textbf{Exception events are the minimal sufficient signal}: ${\geq}$99.33\% across all four models and all seeds tested (1.5B--13B, three families), with ${\sim}$91\% semantic rather than format-driven (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}, \S\ref{sec:nomarker}). Cross-dataset evaluation on DebugBench ($N{=}426$) preserves the ranking, though margins narrow from ceiling effects (\S\ref{sec:debugbench}).
28	\item \textbf{Approximate quantitative decomposition of the full-trace performance gap}: On Qwen-7B (3 seeds), the gap decomposes into gradient dilution (${\sim}$24\%) and information overload (${\sim}$76\%), implying content selection matters more than loss engineering. A budget sweep across four models reveals a phase transition at ${\sim}$500 tail tokens (\S\ref{sec:density}, \S\ref{sec:trace_length}).
29	\item \textbf{Two-tier diagnostic hierarchy}: Tier~1 signals (exceptions, assertions) generalize across all four models (${\geq}$99.33\%), while Tier~2 (loop compression) is model-dependent: Qwen +10.9/+11.0pp (7B/1.5B), DeepSeek +7.9pp, CodeLlama +0.6pp over no trace (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).
30	\end{enumerate}

\section{Introduction}

Execution traces (line-by-line records of a program's runtime behavior) have emerged as a promising input modality for code language models \citep{chen2025tracepile,ding2024traced,wang2025dcsh,ni2024next}.
Yet feeding thousands of trace lines to a model can be no better than feeding none: the diagnostic signal drowns in routine execution steps.
\emph{Which trace components actually carry the signal that matters?}

Prior work found no single trace representation consistently outperforms others \citep{wang2025dcsh}, but focused on generation-oriented tasks.
\emph{Verdict prediction}---classifying whether a test passes or fails---offers a cleaner testbed: as binary classification, it isolates the learning signal from generation noise, enabling controlled component ablation.
As fault detection, the model need not simulate execution, only determine whether something went wrong---and if that signal is concentrated in a small trace subset, information density should matter more than quantity.

We test this hypothesis through the first systematic component ablation of trace representations for verdict prediction.
Using 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program}, we decompose a multi-component trace representation (VOTA: exception events + assertion-point comparisons + loop compression) into individual components across four models spanning 1.5B to 13B parameters and three architecture families: Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B/1.5B-Instruct \citep{qwen2025coder}, CodeLlama-13B-Instruct \citep{roziere2024code}, and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct \citep{deepseek2024coder}.
The results are striking: complete traces (${\sim}$80\%) underperform a single compact component (${\geq}$99\%) despite containing strictly more information---a direct demonstration that information density, not quantity, determines learning efficiency.

\textbf{Exception events alone achieve ${\geq}$99.33\% verdict accuracy across all four models and all seeds tested} (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).
This near-perfect accuracy holds from 1.5B to 13B parameters, while the code-only baseline (\texttt{no\_trace}) varies from 67.3\% to 76.5\% with strong scale dependence.
Training dynamics confirm the density hypothesis: high-density inputs converge rapidly and stably, while verbose traces oscillate without reaching stable accuracy even when gradient dilution is eliminated (Figure~\ref{fig:training_dynamics}).

Adding trace information beyond exceptions provides no benefit: VOTA (${\geq}$98.57\% across all models, excluding outlier seeds) slightly underperforms \texttt{exception\_only} on Qwen-7B (99.05\% vs.\ 99.83\%), with both conditions achieving near-ceiling accuracy across architectures.
The performance gap approximately decomposes into information overload (${\sim}$76\%) and gradient dilution (${\sim}$24\%) on Qwen-7B (3 seeds).
A tail-truncation budget sweep across four models reveals a phase transition at ${\sim}$500 tokens, with \texttt{tail\_2048} recovering 95--98\% of \texttt{exception\_only}'s accuracy.
Even on silent logic errors (55.5\% of failures), \texttt{exception\_only} maintains 100\% recall because test assertions generate exception events.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Information density determines SFT learning efficiency}: training dynamics directly show that denser trace components learn faster and more stably---\texttt{exception\_only} converges within 50 steps while \texttt{full\_trace} with label-only loss oscillates (82--89\%) without stable convergence. Seed variance negatively correlates with input density ($\sigma{=}$0.00 to 1.12), and SFT closes a 6--49pp zero-shot gap across all models (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics}).
\item \textbf{Exception events are the minimal sufficient signal}: ${\geq}$99.33\% across all four models and all seeds tested (1.5B--13B, three families), with ${\sim}$91\% semantic rather than format-driven (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}, \S\ref{sec:nomarker}). Cross-dataset evaluation on DebugBench ($N{=}426$) preserves the ranking, though margins narrow from ceiling effects (\S\ref{sec:debugbench}).
\item \textbf{Approximate quantitative decomposition of the full-trace performance gap}: On Qwen-7B (3 seeds), the gap decomposes into gradient dilution (${\sim}$24\%) and information overload (${\sim}$76\%), implying content selection matters more than loss engineering. A budget sweep across four models reveals a phase transition at ${\sim}$500 tail tokens (\S\ref{sec:density}, \S\ref{sec:trace_length}).
\item \textbf{Two-tier diagnostic hierarchy}: Tier~1 signals (exceptions, assertions) generalize across all four models (${\geq}$99.33\%), while Tier~2 (loop compression) is model-dependent: Qwen +10.9/+11.0pp (7B/1.5B), DeepSeek +7.9pp, CodeLlama +0.6pp over no trace (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).
\end{enumerate}

1	\section{Related Work}
2	
3	\paragraph{Execution Traces for Code LLMs.}
4	TracePile \citep{chen2025tracepile} scaled trace-augmented training to 2.6M samples; \citet{wang2025dcsh} found trace utility task- and format-dependent, which we extend by identifying exception events as the dominant signal.
5	NExT \citep{ni2024next} and ET-CoT \citep{eguchi2025etcot} used trace chain-of-thought for repair and execution reasoning; \citet{ferrando2025execute} found compact traces comparable to full traces, supporting our density finding.
6	\citet{liu2023codeexecution} pre-trained on execution traces; CRUXEval \citep{gu2024cruxeval}, extended to 19 languages \citep{xu2025cruxevalx}, established execution reasoning benchmarks.
7	None decompose which trace components contribute to \emph{classification} accuracy.
8	
9	\paragraph{Code Verdict and Patch Classification.}
10	TRACED \citep{ding2024traced} showed execution-aware pretraining improves vulnerability detection; DeepDFA \citep{steenhoek2024deepdfa} and learned program slicing \citep{yadavally2024slicing} combined classical analysis with deep learning.
11	In patch correctness, \citet{tian2020patchcorrectness}, CC2Vec \citep{hoang2020cc2vec}, LLM4PatchCorrect \citep{zhou2024llm4patch} (84.4\%), and APPT \citep{appt2024} (79.7\%) developed representation learning of code changes.
12	Verdict prediction is an instance of the longstanding test oracle problem \citep{barr2015oracle}; FuseFL \citep{widyasari2024fusefl} and \citet{foster2025mutation} demonstrated structured fault signals; the equivalent-mutant problem \citep{papadakis2019mutation} poses an analogous classification challenge.
13	None isolate individual trace components or compare against rule-based baselines.
14	
15	\paragraph{Fault Localization.}
16	Spectrum-based fault localization (SBFL) ranks program elements by suspiciousness from test spectra \citep{abreu2007accuracy,jones2002visualization,wong2014dstar}; recent LLM-based approaches \citep{kang2024autofl,qin2024agentfl} share our insight that anomalous execution events carry the strongest diagnostic signal, with verdict prediction serving as a prerequisite to FL.
17	
18	\paragraph{Trace Compression and Selection.}
19	TraceCoder \citep{huang2026tracecoder} and InspectCoder \citep{wang2025inspectcoder} use selective trace extraction; RepairAgent \citep{bouzenia2025repairagent} and Agentless \citep{xia2024agentless} incorporate execution feedback in repair workflows, as do SWE-agent \citep{yang2024sweagent} and OpenHands \citep{wang2025openhands}; in the SWE-bench ecosystem \citep{jimenez2024swebench}, these agents rely on test verdict signals to guide patch selection, yet which trace components carry that signal most efficiently remains unstudied.
20	In the prompt compression literature, LLMLingua \citep{jiang2023llmlingua} and Selective Context \citep{li2023selectivecontext} showed that pruning low-information tokens preserves downstream accuracy, corroborating our finding that compact trace formats outperform verbose ones; \citet{haque2025traces} found raw traces provide limited repair benefit.
21	Our approximate decomposition (gradient dilution ${\sim}$24\% vs.\ information overload ${\sim}$76\%) provides the first quantitative framework for \emph{why} compression helps, complementing these methods' focus on \emph{how}.
22	
23	\paragraph{Calibration and Defect Prediction.}
24	Neural network calibration \citep{guo2017calibration}, extended to LLMs \citep{kadavath2022language,geng2024calibration,spiess2025calibration}, studies confidence-correctness alignment; our ECE ${<}$ 0.007 suggests compact inputs improve calibration. Just-in-time defect prediction \citep{kamei2013large,hoang2019deepjit,pornprasit2021jitline} shares our fault detection motivation but operates on code change features.
25	
26	\paragraph{Training Efficiency and Data Selection.}
27	Curriculum learning \citep{bengio2009curriculum}, dataset cartography via training dynamics \citep{swayamdipta2020cartography}, and data selection methods \citep{sachdeva2024dataefficient,xie2023doremi} show that data quality and ordering improve convergence, consistent with our finding that compact exceptions enable rapid convergence while verbose traces trap the model in oscillation.
28

1	\section{Method}
2	
3	\subsection{Task Definition}
4	
5	We study \emph{verdict prediction}: given a Python function, a test input, and an optional execution trace, predict whether the test passes or fails.
6	The model produces a single token (\texttt{pass} or \texttt{fail}), making this a binary classification task.
7	Unlike code generation \citep{chen2025tracepile} or output prediction \citep{gu2024cruxeval}, verdict prediction isolates the model's ability to detect faults from its ability to simulate execution.
8	The discrete binary outcome makes the effect of each trace component directly measurable, providing cleaner ablation contrasts than generation tasks where output quality varies continuously.
9	
10	\subsection{Dataset}
11	\label{sec:dataset}
12	
13	We sampled 10 candidate solutions per problem from Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct (temperature 0.8, top\_p 0.95) for 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} (164) and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program} (427), executed each against canonical tests with \texttt{sys.settrace} to obtain line-level traces and pass/fail verdicts, yielding 5,910 pairs (67\% pass, 33\% fail).
14	The dataset is split 80/20 by problem ID into 4,720 training and 1,190 test samples (majority baseline: 71.51\%).
15	The \texttt{exception\_only} format collapses passing solutions into identical rows (39.45\% train, 48.99\% test duplicates); these duplicates arise from multiple candidate solutions per problem, with the train--test split enforced at the problem level (472 train / 119 test problems, zero crossover; Appendix~\ref{sec:dedup_stats}).
16	
17	\subsection{Trace Representations}
18	
19	We define seven conditions that vary the trace information available (Figure~\ref{fig:trace_overview}):
20	\begin{itemize}
21	\item \texttt{no\_trace}: Source code and test input only.
22	\item \texttt{full\_trace}: Complete line-by-line trace with variable states.
23	\item \texttt{VOTA}: Exception events + assertion-point comparisons + loop compression (Appendix~\ref{sec:vota_algorithm}).
24	\item \texttt{exception\_only}: Only exception/error events.
25	\item \texttt{ae\_only}: Only assertion-point actual/expected pairs.
26	\item \texttt{loop\_only}: Only loop compression summaries.
27	\item \texttt{VOTA\_no\_ae}: VOTA without assertion-point information.
28	\end{itemize}
29	
30	\begin{figure*}[t]
31	\centering
32	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig1_trace_overview}
33	\caption{Overview of the verdict prediction pipeline. Source code and a test input are executed to produce a full raw trace. Four conditions vary the trace information: \texttt{no\_trace} (75.13\%), \texttt{full\_trace} (81.76\%), VOTA (99.41\%), and \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%). Accuracies for Qwen-2.5-7B (seed=42, $N{=}1{,}190$). Appendix~\ref{sec:vota_examples} provides input/output examples.}
34	\label{fig:trace_overview}
35	\end{figure*}
36	
37	\subsection{Models and Training}
38	
39	We evaluate four models spanning three architecture families: \textbf{Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B/1.5B-Instruct} \citep{qwen2025coder}, \textbf{CodeLlama-13B-Instruct} \citep{roziere2024code}, and \textbf{DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct} \citep{deepseek2024coder}, covering a 1.5B--13B parameter range (8.7$\times$).
40	All conditions use LoRA \citep{hu2022lora} (rank=16, $\alpha$=32, dropout=0.05) on all linear layers, 3 epochs, effective batch size 32, LR $2 \times 10^{-4}$ with linear warmup/decay, max sequence length 2{,}048 tokens.
41	Sequences exceeding this limit are truncated while preserving the verdict label.
42	The primary seed is 42; seeds 123 and 456 test \texttt{exception\_only} robustness (Appendix~\ref{sec:training_details}).
43	
44	\subsection{Loss Ablation}
45	
46	To disentangle training signal from input signal quality, we introduce \texttt{full\_trace\_label\_only}: identical full-trace input but loss computed only on the verdict token (trace positions masked).
47	Improvement over standard \texttt{full\_trace} is attributable to \emph{gradient dilution}; the remaining gap to VOTA reflects \emph{information overload} at inference time.
48

1	\section{Experiments}
2	
3	We evaluate across two research questions:
4	(1)~Do Tier~1 exception signals generalize across models?
5	(2)~What is the relative contribution of each trace component?
6	All experiments use $N{=}1{,}190$ test samples; accuracy is reported with Wilson 95\% CIs.\footnote{Data is partitioned at the problem level (472 train / 119 test problems, zero crossover; \S\ref{sec:dataset}). The \texttt{exception\_only} format collapses passing solutions into identical rows (48.99\% test duplicates; Appendix~\ref{sec:dedup_stats}), but these arise from within-problem variants, not cross-set leakage; deduplication sensitivity analysis confirms 0.00pp delta across all 19 experimental conditions.}
7	Pairwise comparisons use paired bootstrap resampling ($B{=}10{,}000$, seed=42); all differences are significant at $p{<}.0001$ unless noted.
8	
9	\subsection{Cross-Model Comparison}
10	\label{sec:cross_model}
11	
12	Table~\ref{tab:cross_model} compares four models spanning an 8.7$\times$ parameter range (1.5B--13B) and three architecture families (Qwen, DeepSeek, CodeLlama) under key conditions.
13	
14	\begin{table}[t]
15	\centering
16	\caption{Cross-model verdict accuracy (\%, $N{=}1{,}190$) across four models (1.5B--13B) and three architecture families. Multi-seed entries report mean$\pm$std over 3 seeds. Bold: best per model. Full per-seed breakdowns in Appendix~\ref{sec:full_results}; per-class metrics in Appendix~\ref{sec:per_class}.}
17	\label{tab:cross_model}
18	\small
19	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
20	\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
21	\toprule
22	\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Qwen-7B} & \textbf{Qwen-1.5B} & \textbf{CL-13B} & \textbf{DS-6.7B} \\
23	\midrule
24	exception\_only & \textbf{99.83}{\scriptsize$\pm$0.00} & \textbf{99.83}{\scriptsize$\pm$0.00} & \textbf{99.89}{\scriptsize$\pm$0.10} & \textbf{99.39}{\scriptsize$\pm$0.10} \\
25	ae\_only & 99.64{\scriptsize$\pm$0.49} & --- & --- & 98.74 \\
26	VOTA & 99.05{\scriptsize$\pm$0.38} & 99.58 & 98.57 & 99.25$^\ddag$ \\
27	loop\_only & 86.05{\scriptsize$\pm$0.52} & 78.32 & 77.06 & 81.26 \\
28	no\_trace & 75.13 & 67.31 & 76.47 & 73.36 \\
29	\midrule
30	Majority baseline & \multicolumn{4}{c}{71.51} \\
31	\bottomrule
32	\end{tabular}%
33	}
34	\vspace{2pt}
35	\par\raggedright\footnotesize
36	DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} 3 seeds: 99.33/99.50/99.33 ($\sigma{=}$0.10pp).
37	VOTA on Qwen-7B: 99.41/98.66/99.08 ($\sigma{=}$0.38).
38	\texttt{ae\_only} 3 seeds: 99.92/99.08/99.92 (mean 99.64\%); Qwen-7B \texttt{loop\_only} 3 seeds: 85.63/85.88/86.64 (mean 86.05\%).
39	Qwen-1.5B \texttt{exception\_only}: 99.83\% across 3 seeds ($\sigma{=}$0).
40	$^\ddag$DeepSeek VOTA 3 seeds: 84.45/99.16/99.33; seed 42 (84.45\%, fail recall\,=\,45.4\%) is a training failure due to tokenizer-driven truncation (Appendix~\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}), reported as 2-seed mean.
41	\end{table}
42	
43	\paragraph{Exception dominance across families.}
44	Under \texttt{exception\_only}, all four models achieve ${\geq}$99.33\% across all seeds: Qwen-7B (99.83\%$\pm$0.00, 3 seeds), Qwen-1.5B (99.83\%), CodeLlama-13B (99.89\%$\pm$0.10, 3 seeds; seed 123 achieves 100\%), and DeepSeek-6.7B (99.39\%$\pm$0.10, 3 seeds).
45	The cross-model range is 0.50pp (99.39--99.89\%), the tightest of any condition.
46	
47	\paragraph{Scale invariance of exception signals.}
48	Exception-based accuracy is shared by models spanning 1.5B to 13B parameters (8.7$\times$): both Qwen-1.5B and CodeLlama-13B achieve 99.83\%+ on the same representation.
49	CodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\% (0/1190 errors), confirming that Qwen's two persistent errors (from \texttt{GeneratorExit}; Appendix~\ref{sec:irreducible}) are high-probability convergence artifacts rather than hard data limitations.
50	In contrast, \texttt{no\_trace} scales monotonically with capacity: 67.31\% (1.5B) $\to$ 75.13\% (7B) $\to$ 76.47\% (13B), a 9.16pp range that exception events completely eliminate (Figure~\ref{fig:cross_scale}).
51	
52	\begin{figure}[t]
53	\centering
54	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig3_cross_model_gap}
55	\caption{Verdict accuracy vs.\ model scale. \texttt{exception\_only} maintains ${\geq}$99.33\% regardless of scale (1.5B--13B), while \texttt{no\_trace} shows monotonic scale sensitivity (+9.16pp from 1.5B to 13B). The \texttt{nomarker} condition (format markers removed) shows no degradation at smaller scale (${\sim}$97.7--97.8\%).}
56	\label{fig:cross_scale}
57	\end{figure}
58	
59	\paragraph{VOTA cross-family variation.}
60	Excluding outlier seeds, VOTA achieves ${\geq}$98.57\% across all four models: 99.58\% (Qwen-1.5B) $>$ 99.25\%$\pm$0.12 (DeepSeek-6.7B, 2 seeds) $>$ 99.05\%$\pm$0.38 (Qwen-7B, 3 seeds) $>$ 98.57\% (CodeLlama-13B; CI [97.9, 99.2]), a 1.01pp range.
61	DeepSeek seed 42 (84.45\%, fail recall = 45.4\%) is a training failure driven by tokenizer-induced truncation (91.7\% of training samples affected; Appendix~\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}); the remaining seeds (99.16\%, 99.33\%) match cross-model performance.
62	\texttt{exception\_only} inputs are compact (median 150 tokens), sidestepping truncation entirely (Appendix~\ref{sec:robustness_analysis}).
63	
64	\subsection{Component Ablation}
65	\label{sec:ablation}
66	
67	Multi-seed \texttt{ae\_only} ablations use Qwen-7B; \texttt{loop\_only} is evaluated across three models to test Tier~2 generalization (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}).
68	Table~\ref{tab:ablation} decomposes VOTA on Qwen-2.5-7B and reveals a two-tier hierarchy: Tier~1 (\texttt{exception\_only}) generalizes across all four models (${\geq}$99.33\%), while Tier~2 (\texttt{loop\_only}) is model-dependent.
69	
70	\begin{table}[t]
71	\centering
72	\caption{Component ablation on Qwen-2.5-7B ($N{=}1{,}190$). Tier~1 signals achieve near-perfect accuracy; combining them (VOTA) slightly dilutes performance. Entries marked $^\dag$/$^\S$/$^\ddag$ are 3-seed mean$\pm$std; per-seed breakdowns in Appendix~\ref{sec:full_results}. Seed $\sigma$ negatively correlates with density (0.00 for exception to 0.52 for loop).}
73	\label{tab:ablation}
74	\small
75	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
76	\begin{tabular}{llccc}
77	\toprule
78	\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Components} & \textbf{Acc (\%)} & \textbf{95\% CI} & \textbf{Tier} \\
79	\midrule
80	ae\_only & assertion-point & 99.64$^\dag$ & [99.26, 99.87] & 1 \\
81	exception\_only & exception events & \textbf{99.83} & [99.58, 100.00] & 1 \\
82	VOTA & exc+ae+loop & 99.05$^\S$ & [98.49, 99.50] & --- \\
83	VOTA\_no\_ae & exc+loop & 99.41 & [98.90, 99.80] & --- \\
84	loop\_only & loop compression & 86.05$^\ddag$ & [83.97, 87.96] & 2 \\
85	full\_trace & complete trace & 81.76 & [79.70, 83.90] & --- \\
86	no\_trace & none & 75.13 & [72.77, 77.48] & --- \\
87	\midrule
88	Regex (best) & exc.\ type regex & 93.61 & --- & --- \\
89	3-shot (Qwen-7B) & in-context learning & 90.84 & --- & --- \\
90	Zero-shot (4 models) & prompting & 51.0--93.5 & --- & --- \\
91	\bottomrule
92	\end{tabular}%
93	}
94	\end{table}
95	
96	Tier~1 signals are individually sufficient: \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%$\pm$0.00) exceeds VOTA (99.05\%$\pm$0.38) by +0.78pp (2/3 seeds $p{<}.05$, all directionally consistent), implying that combining signals introduces noise.
97	Removing assertion points has no effect (\texttt{VOTA\_no\_ae} = 99.41\%, single seed), confirming exception dominance.
98	The Tier~1/2 boundary is unambiguous: the lowest Tier~1 condition (\texttt{ae\_only} on DeepSeek, 98.74\%, CI [98.07, 99.33]) exceeds the highest Tier~2 (\texttt{loop\_only} on Qwen-7B, 86.05\%, CI [83.97, 87.96]) by 12.69\,pp with non-overlapping confidence intervals.
99	Tier~2 \texttt{loop\_only} lifts over \texttt{no\_trace} are model-dependent: both Qwen models show consistent benefit (+10.92pp at 7B, +11.01pp at 1.5B, $p{<}.0001$), DeepSeek +7.90pp (81.26\%, CI [79.08, 83.45]), CodeLlama +0.59pp (77.06\%, n.s.).
100	\paragraph{Rule-based baseline comparison.}

111	\label{sec:nomarker}
112

114	To quantify the marker's contribution, we retrain with all format markers removed (\texttt{nomarker} condition).
115	
116	Qwen-7B 3-seed mean: 97.65\% $\pm$ 0.96 (seeds 42/123/456: 96.55/98.32/98.07\%), a drop of 2.18pp from \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%).
117	Qwen-1.5B: 97.82\%, drop of 2.01pp.

122	\label{sec:density}

127	\centering
128	\caption{Approximate information density decomposition: gradient dilution (${\sim}$24\%) vs.\ information overload (${\sim}$76\%). \texttt{label\_only} and VOTA are 3-seed means on Qwen-7B.}

\section{Experiments}

We evaluate across two research questions:
(1)~Do Tier~1 exception signals generalize across models?
(2)~What is the relative contribution of each trace component?
All experiments use $N{=}1{,}190$ test samples; accuracy is reported with Wilson 95\% CIs.\footnote{Data is partitioned at the problem level (472 train / 119 test problems, zero crossover; \S\ref{sec:dataset}). The \texttt{exception\_only} format collapses passing solutions into identical rows (48.99\% test duplicates; Appendix~\ref{sec:dedup_stats}), but these arise from within-problem variants, not cross-set leakage; deduplication sensitivity analysis confirms 0.00pp delta across all 19 experimental conditions.}
Pairwise comparisons use paired bootstrap resampling ($B{=}10{,}000$, seed=42); all differences are significant at $p{<}.0001$ unless noted.

\subsection{Cross-Model Comparison}
\label{sec:cross_model}

Table~\ref{tab:cross_model} compares four models spanning an 8.7$\times$ parameter range (1.5B--13B) and three architecture families (Qwen, DeepSeek, CodeLlama) under key conditions.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Cross-model verdict accuracy (\%, $N{=}1{,}190$) across four models (1.5B--13B) and three architecture families. Multi-seed entries report mean$\pm$std over 3 seeds. Bold: best per model. Full per-seed breakdowns in Appendix~\ref{sec:full_results}; per-class metrics in Appendix~\ref{sec:per_class}.}
\label{tab:cross_model}
\small
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Qwen-7B} & \textbf{Qwen-1.5B} & \textbf{CL-13B} & \textbf{DS-6.7B} \\
\midrule
exception\_only & \textbf{99.83}{\scriptsize$\pm$0.00} & \textbf{99.83}{\scriptsize$\pm$0.00} & \textbf{99.89}{\scriptsize$\pm$0.10} & \textbf{99.39}{\scriptsize$\pm$0.10} \\
ae\_only & 99.64{\scriptsize$\pm$0.49} & --- & --- & 98.74 \\
VOTA & 99.05{\scriptsize$\pm$0.38} & 99.58 & 98.57 & 99.25$^\ddag$ \\
loop\_only & 86.05{\scriptsize$\pm$0.52} & 78.32 & 77.06 & 81.26 \\
no\_trace & 75.13 & 67.31 & 76.47 & 73.36 \\
\midrule
Majority baseline & \multicolumn{4}{c}{71.51} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}%
}
\vspace{2pt}
\par\raggedright\footnotesize
DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} 3 seeds: 99.33/99.50/99.33 ($\sigma{=}$0.10pp).
VOTA on Qwen-7B: 99.41/98.66/99.08 ($\sigma{=}$0.38).
\texttt{ae\_only} 3 seeds: 99.92/99.08/99.92 (mean 99.64\%); Qwen-7B \texttt{loop\_only} 3 seeds: 85.63/85.88/86.64 (mean 86.05\%).
Qwen-1.5B \texttt{exception\_only}: 99.83\% across 3 seeds ($\sigma{=}$0).
$^\ddag$DeepSeek VOTA 3 seeds: 84.45/99.16/99.33; seed 42 (84.45\%, fail recall\,=\,45.4\%) is a training failure due to tokenizer-driven truncation (Appendix~\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}), reported as 2-seed mean.
\end{table}

\paragraph{Exception dominance across families.}
Under \texttt{exception\_only}, all four models achieve ${\geq}$99.33\% across all seeds: Qwen-7B (99.83\%$\pm$0.00, 3 seeds), Qwen-1.5B (99.83\%), CodeLlama-13B (99.89\%$\pm$0.10, 3 seeds; seed 123 achieves 100\%), and DeepSeek-6.7B (99.39\%$\pm$0.10, 3 seeds).
The cross-model range is 0.50pp (99.39--99.89\%), the tightest of any condition.

\paragraph{Scale invariance of exception signals.}
Exception-based accuracy is shared by models spanning 1.5B to 13B parameters (8.7$\times$): both Qwen-1.5B and CodeLlama-13B achieve 99.83\%+ on the same representation.
CodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\% (0/1190 errors), confirming that Qwen's two persistent errors (from \texttt{GeneratorExit}; Appendix~\ref{sec:irreducible}) are high-probability convergence artifacts rather than hard data limitations.
In contrast, \texttt{no\_trace} scales monotonically with capacity: 67.31\% (1.5B) $\to$ 75.13\% (7B) $\to$ 76.47\% (13B), a 9.16pp range that exception events completely eliminate (Figure~\ref{fig:cross_scale}).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig3_cross_model_gap}
\caption{Verdict accuracy vs.\ model scale. \texttt{exception\_only} maintains ${\geq}$99.33\% regardless of scale (1.5B--13B), while \texttt{no\_trace} shows monotonic scale sensitivity (+9.16pp from 1.5B to 13B). The \texttt{nomarker} condition (format markers removed) shows no degradation at smaller scale (${\sim}$97.7--97.8\%).}
\label{fig:cross_scale}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{VOTA cross-family variation.}
Excluding outlier seeds, VOTA achieves ${\geq}$98.57\% across all four models: 99.58\% (Qwen-1.5B) $>$ 99.25\%$\pm$0.12 (DeepSeek-6.7B, 2 seeds) $>$ 99.05\%$\pm$0.38 (Qwen-7B, 3 seeds) $>$ 98.57\% (CodeLlama-13B; CI [97.9, 99.2]), a 1.01pp range.
DeepSeek seed 42 (84.45\%, fail recall = 45.4\%) is a training failure driven by tokenizer-induced truncation (91.7\% of training samples affected; Appendix~\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}); the remaining seeds (99.16\%, 99.33\%) match cross-model performance.
\texttt{exception\_only} inputs are compact (median 150 tokens), sidestepping truncation entirely (Appendix~\ref{sec:robustness_analysis}).

\subsection{Component Ablation}
\label{sec:ablation}

Multi-seed \texttt{ae\_only} ablations use Qwen-7B; \texttt{loop\_only} is evaluated across three models to test Tier~2 generalization (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}).
Table~\ref{tab:ablation} decomposes VOTA on Qwen-2.5-7B and reveals a two-tier hierarchy: Tier~1 (\texttt{exception\_only}) generalizes across all four models (${\geq}$99.33\%), while Tier~2 (\texttt{loop\_only}) is model-dependent.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Component ablation on Qwen-2.5-7B ($N{=}1{,}190$). Tier~1 signals achieve near-perfect accuracy; combining them (VOTA) slightly dilutes performance. Entries marked $^\dag$/$^\S$/$^\ddag$ are 3-seed mean$\pm$std; per-seed breakdowns in Appendix~\ref{sec:full_results}. Seed $\sigma$ negatively correlates with density (0.00 for exception to 0.52 for loop).}
\label{tab:ablation}
\small
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Components} & \textbf{Acc (\%)} & \textbf{95\% CI} & \textbf{Tier} \\
\midrule
ae\_only & assertion-point & 99.64$^\dag$ & [99.26, 99.87] & 1 \\
exception\_only & exception events & \textbf{99.83} & [99.58, 100.00] & 1 \\
VOTA & exc+ae+loop & 99.05$^\S$ & [98.49, 99.50] & --- \\
VOTA\_no\_ae & exc+loop & 99.41 & [98.90, 99.80] & --- \\
loop\_only & loop compression & 86.05$^\ddag$ & [83.97, 87.96] & 2 \\
full\_trace & complete trace & 81.76 & [79.70, 83.90] & --- \\
no\_trace & none & 75.13 & [72.77, 77.48] & --- \\
\midrule
Regex (best) & exc.\ type regex & 93.61 & --- & --- \\
3-shot (Qwen-7B) & in-context learning & 90.84 & --- & --- \\
Zero-shot (4 models) & prompting & 51.0--93.5 & --- & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}%
}
\end{table}

Tier~1 signals are individually sufficient: \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%$\pm$0.00) exceeds VOTA (99.05\%$\pm$0.38) by +0.78pp (2/3 seeds $p{<}.05$, all directionally consistent), implying that combining signals introduces noise.
Removing assertion points has no effect (\texttt{VOTA\_no\_ae} = 99.41\%, single seed), confirming exception dominance.
The Tier~1/2 boundary is unambiguous: the lowest Tier~1 condition (\texttt{ae\_only} on DeepSeek, 98.74\%, CI [98.07, 99.33]) exceeds the highest Tier~2 (\texttt{loop\_only} on Qwen-7B, 86.05\%, CI [83.97, 87.96]) by 12.69\,pp with non-overlapping confidence intervals.
Tier~2 \texttt{loop\_only} lifts over \texttt{no\_trace} are model-dependent: both Qwen models show consistent benefit (+10.92pp at 7B, +11.01pp at 1.5B, $p{<}.0001$), DeepSeek +7.90pp (81.26\%, CI [79.08, 83.45]), CodeLlama +0.59pp (77.06\%, n.s.).
\paragraph{Rule-based baseline comparison.}
The strongest non-trivial regex heuristic (B4: exception class name matching; Table~\ref{tab:regex}) achieves 93.61\% accuracy (F1=0.876), trailing SFT \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%, F1=0.997) by 6.22pp (McNemar $p{<}.001$).
The gap concentrates on caught-exception boundary cases: regex flags all exception events as failures, while SFT learns to distinguish caught exceptions (benign, inside \texttt{try/except}) from uncaught faults, correctly resolving 6/8 boundary samples (Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).
Across all formats, SFT outperforms the best applicable regex by +3.62--23.86pp (Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).

\paragraph{Zero-shot and few-shot LLM baselines.}
Zero-shot prompting spans 51.0--93.5\% across four models (42.44pp range), with performance uncorrelated with model size (Qwen-1.5B: 93.45\% vs.\ CodeLlama-13B: 51.01\%).
Three-shot ICL on Qwen-7B (90.84\%) improves only 1.76pp and still trails SFT by 8.99pp.
SFT compresses this 42.44pp range to 0.50pp (99.39--99.89\%), closing a 6--49pp gap with 4,720 training samples (Appendix~\ref{sec:zeroshot_cross_model}).

\subsection{Format Marker Ablation}
\label{sec:nomarker}

The \texttt{exception\_only} format includes a \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} marker in all pass-class samples (regex baseline B5 exploits this for 99.33\% accuracy; Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).
To quantify the marker's contribution, we retrain with all format markers removed (\texttt{nomarker} condition).

Qwen-7B 3-seed mean: 97.65\% $\pm$ 0.96 (seeds 42/123/456: 96.55/98.32/98.07\%), a drop of 2.18pp from \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%).
Qwen-1.5B: 97.82\%, drop of 2.01pp.
The marker contribution (${\sim}$2pp) accounts for only ${\sim}$9\% of the total exception lift over \texttt{no\_trace} (24.70pp on 7B).
Exception events thus provide two signal layers that show no degradation at smaller scale: structural markers (${\sim}$2pp, regex-learnable) and semantic exception content (${\sim}$22pp, requiring SFT to distinguish caught from uncaught exceptions).

\subsection{Information Density Decomposition}
\label{sec:density}

The 17.29pp gap between \texttt{full\_trace} (81.76\%) and VOTA (99.05\%, 3-seed mean) decomposes via \texttt{full\_trace\_label\_only} (85.94\%$\pm$1.12, 3 seeds; Table~\ref{tab:density}), which retains the full trace but masks all trace tokens from the loss.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Approximate information density decomposition: gradient dilution (${\sim}$24\%) vs.\ information overload (${\sim}$76\%). \texttt{label\_only} and VOTA are 3-seed means on Qwen-7B.}
\label{tab:density}
\small
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Acc (\%)} & \textbf{$\Delta$ vs.\ full\_trace} & \textbf{Gap explained} \\
\midrule
full\_trace & 81.76 & --- & --- \\
label\_only & 85.94{\scriptsize$\pm$1.12} & +4.18pp & 24\% \\
VOTA & 99.05{\scriptsize$\pm$0.38} & +17.29pp & 100\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}%
}
\end{table}

Gradient dilution accounts for approximately 24\% of the gap (+4.18pp, 3-seed mean): when the model no longer wastes gradient updates on predicting trace tokens, accuracy improves even with identical input.
The remaining ${\sim}$76\% (+13.11pp) reflects information overload at inference: the model receives thousands of irrelevant trace lines that compete for attention with the diagnostic signal, regardless of loss design.
This asymmetry implies that content selection matters more than loss engineering.
Cross-model evidence supports this: the tail-truncation phase transition at ${\sim}$500 tokens (\S\ref{sec:trace_length}, all four models) coincides with exception traceback length, indicating that retaining diagnostic content is the critical factor.
This is further corroborated by the DeepSeek label-only collapse: applying label-only loss to full traces with 91.7\% truncation causes complete model failure (28.5\% accuracy), confirming that information density in trace content is the binding constraint.
The two factors may interact, and label-only loss simultaneously changes multiple optimization dynamics; the 24\%/76\% attribution is an approximate decomposition (3 seeds, single model).

\subsection{Additional Analyses}
\label{sec:additional}

\paragraph{Trace length ablation.}
\label{sec:trace_length}
Varying the head-truncated trace token budget (256--no limit) on Qwen-7B yields accuracy in a narrow 77.2\%--81.8\% band with a non-monotonic pattern: 1024-token prefixes (77.23\%) underperform 512-token prefixes (80.42\%, $p{=}.002$), because mid-length prefixes retain enough irrelevant content to mislead the model while discarding diagnostic events near the trace terminus (Appendix~\ref{sec:trace_length_full}).
This non-monotonicity is specific to head-truncation; under tail-truncation, accuracy increases monotonically for two of three models (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model} in Appendix), with only DeepSeek showing a mild architecture-specific reversal at tail-1024$\to$tail-2048 ($-$1.5pp).

\paragraph{Truncation direction and budget curve.}
Tail-truncation (retaining the last $k$ tokens) dramatically outperforms head-truncation: among the three models with complete data, tail-2048 exceeds head-2048 by 15.5--22.6pp, with the gap widening at smaller scale (Qwen-1.5B: +22.6pp vs.\ Qwen-7B: +15.5pp; Appendix~\ref{sec:trace_length_full}, Table~\ref{tab:head_vs_tail}).
All four models' head-2048 accuracies converge into a narrow 75.3--81.8\% band (6.5pp), comparable to the tail-256 band (72.6--78.9\%, 6.3pp), indicating that signal-poor conditions produce a shared performance floor regardless of scale or architecture.

A cross-model budget sweep across four models and three architecture families reveals a phase transition localized between 384 and 512 tail tokens.
At tail-384, all models remain near baseline (73.6--82.9\%, only +1.0--6.5pp over tail-256); the steep jump occurs at 384$\to$512 (+11.0--22.0pp), crossing from near-baseline to near-ceiling (${\sim}$94--98\%).
This localizes the critical threshold to ${\sim}$400--500 tokens, matching the typical exception traceback length (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model}).
Beyond 512 tokens, accuracy converges further: multi-seed validation across all 12 model$\times$seed combinations confirms all tail-512 accuracies fall within a 4.63pp band [93.61\%, 98.24\%] (Table~\ref{tab:tail512_seeds}); at tail-1024, three models reach 96.5--98.2\%, compressing the 6.3pp cross-model spread observed at tail-256.
\texttt{tail\_2048} captures 95--98\% of \texttt{exception\_only}'s accuracy across all completed configurations.
The residual 2--5pp gap confirms that semantic extraction (identifying exception type and message) still outperforms positional extraction (retaining a fixed window containing non-diagnostic lines).

\paragraph{Calibration.}
\label{sec:calibration}
Calibration mirrors the tier hierarchy: \texttt{exception\_only} achieves ECE = 0.0027 vs.\ 0.171 for \texttt{no\_trace}, a 63$\times$ gap (Figure~\ref{fig:calibration}).
This calibration advantage generalizes across architectures and scales: all four models (1.5B--13B) achieve ECE ${<}$ 0.007 under \texttt{exception\_only} (Appendix~\ref{sec:calibration_full}).

\paragraph{Error orthogonality.}
\texttt{exception\_only}'s 2 errors have zero overlap with all other conditions' error sets (Jaccard = 0.000), confirming it operates on an independent signal dimension (Appendix~\ref{sec:error_overlap}).

\paragraph{Exception type breakdown.}
A per-exception-type breakdown (Appendix~\ref{sec:exception_type}) confirms that all standard exception types achieve 100\% accuracy; the only failures arise from \texttt{GeneratorExit}, a benign \texttt{BaseException} subclass.

\paragraph{Cross-dataset generalization.}
\label{sec:debugbench}
On DebugBench \citep{tian2024debugbench} ($N{=}426$), the ranking is preserved: \texttt{exception\_only} 100\%, VOTA 99.77\%, \texttt{no\_trace} 96.71\%; narrow margins reflect a ceiling effect from structurally distinctive mutations (Appendix~\ref{sec:debugbench_full}).

6	This density perspective explains three key results: (1)~adding trace information beyond exceptions provides no benefit (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}), because low-density content competes for attention; (2)~a tail-truncation budget sweep reveals a sharp phase transition at ${\sim}$500 tokens (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model}), matching the boundary where diagnostic events dominate; (3)~the SFT advantage over regex concentrates on caught-exception boundary cases, confirming semantic signal extraction (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).

17	Zero-shot prompting spans a 42pp range across models (\S\ref{sec:additional}), which SFT compresses to sub-1pp; few-shot ICL improves marginally, confirming the bottleneck is verdict calibration rather than exception recognition.
18	
19	\paragraph{Near-perfect floor, not hard ceiling.}
20	The 2 errors (both \texttt{GeneratorExit}; Appendix~\ref{sec:error_overlap}) are shared across configurations; CodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\%, confirming 99.83\% is a convergence \emph{floor}, signal-limited rather than capacity-limited.
21	
22	\paragraph{Tokenizer efficiency.}
23	CodeLlama's tokenizer produces ${\sim}$20\% more tokens than Qwen's on identical inputs; a label-only loss variant recovers accuracy at tail-1024 but collapses at tail-2048, indicating LoRA long-sequence instability (Appendix~\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}).
24	
25	\paragraph{Tier hierarchy and methodological implications.}
26	The two-tier structure (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) suggests a fallback design: extract exception events first, resort to Tier~2 only when no exception is raised.
27	The near-zero loop benefit on CodeLlama-13B may reflect limited loop-pattern coverage in its pre-training data, combined with a relatively high \texttt{no\_trace} baseline (76.47\%) that leaves minimal headroom for loop-derived signal.
28	Notably, the Qwen family shows consistent loop benefit across scale (1.5B: +11.0pp; 7B: +10.9pp), suggesting that loop signal utilization is an architecture-level property rather than a capacity effect.
29	The methodological insight---that information density determines learning efficiency---transfers to any trace-based task where compact diagnostic events exist within verbose traces, such as re-analyzing archived CI/CD logs when the original test environment is unavailable.
30	
31	\paragraph{Density and cross-model robustness.}
32	Tier~1 and Tier~2 exhibit contrasting cross-model stability (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}): \texttt{exception\_only}'s cross-model range is ${<}$1pp, while \texttt{loop\_only} spans ${\sim}$9pp.
33	However, $N{=}3$ models is insufficient to establish a continuous relationship, and the correlation is confounded: Tier~1 signals are both high-density \emph{and} direct fault indicators, so density cannot be disentangled from signal type.
34	This is further corroborated by a negative result: applying label-only loss to DeepSeek full traces---where 91.7\% of samples are truncated---causes complete model collapse (28.5\% accuracy, eval loss diverges to NaN), confirming that information density in the trace content, not the loss function, is the binding constraint on learning.
35	
36	\paragraph{Exception events capture test verdict signals, not just crashes.}
37	Although 55.5\% of failures are silent logic errors, \texttt{exception\_only} achieves 100\% fail recall because test assertions generate \texttt{AssertionError} events, confirming ``exception events'' encompasses both crashes and assertion failures.

1	\section{Conclusion}
2	
3	We presented the first systematic component ablation for verdict prediction across four models (1.5B--13B, three families), finding that information density determines learning efficiency: compact exception events converge rapidly while verbose traces oscillate without stable convergence.
4	Exception events achieve ${\geq}$99.33\% across all four models with consistent cross-model generalization, while lower-density loop signals are model-dependent; generalization beyond LLM-generated Python code remains open.

103	\section{VOTA Extraction Algorithm}
104	\label{sec:vota_algorithm}
105	
106	Algorithm~\ref{alg:vota} describes the three-component VOTA extraction pipeline applied to a raw \texttt{sys.settrace} execution log.
107	
108	\begin{algorithm}[t]
109	\caption{VOTA Trace Extraction}
110	\label{alg:vota}
111	\small
112	\begin{algorithmic}[1]
113	\REQUIRE Raw trace $T$ from \texttt{sys.settrace} (list of events)
114	\ENSURE Compressed VOTA representation $V$
115	\STATE $V \leftarrow$ empty string
116	\STATE \textbf{// Component 1: Exception summary}
117	\FOR{each event $e$ in $T$ with type \texttt{exception}}
118	  \STATE Parse traceback $\rightarrow$ extract error type, message, file, line
119	  \STATE Append \texttt{[ERROR] type: message (file:line)} to $V$
120	\ENDFOR
121	\IF{no exception events found}
122	  \STATE Append \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} to $V$
123	\ENDIF
124	\STATE \textbf{// Component 2: Assertion-point comparison}
125	\FOR{each \texttt{assert} or \texttt{return} event $e$ in $T$}
126	  \STATE Extract actual value from execution state
127	  \STATE Extract expected value from test assertion
128	  \STATE Append \texttt{[ASSERT] actual=... expected=... match=T/F} to $V$
129	\ENDFOR
130	\STATE \textbf{// Component 3: Loop compression}
131	\FOR{each consecutive repeated line sequence $S$ in $T$}
132	  \IF{$|S| \geq 2$ iterations of same loop body}
133	    \STATE Replace $S$ with single iteration + \texttt{[repeated $\times$N]}
134	  \ENDIF
135	\ENDFOR
136	\STATE Append compressed non-exception lines to $V$
137	\RETURN $V$
138	\end{algorithmic}
139	\end{algorithm}

253	\section{Tokenizer and Truncation Analysis}
254	\label{sec:tokenizer_analysis}
255	
256	DeepSeek VOTA seed 42 (84.45\%) is a training failure driven by tokenizer-induced truncation.
257	Re-evaluation of the seed 42 checkpoint with the standard max\_length=2048 yields 16\% accuracy, confirming complete model collapse rather than marginal degradation.
258	The previously reported 84.45\% was obtained with max\_length=16384, which partially bypasses tokenizer truncation.
259	Seeds 123 and 456, evaluated under identical conditions, achieve 99.16\% and 99.33\% respectively.
260	The DeepSeek tokenizer averages 2{,}626 tokens per VOTA sample versus 1{,}929 for Qwen, causing 91.7\% of DeepSeek VOTA training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window.
261	The training framework preserves the verdict label but truncates trace content, so the model trains with incomplete diagnostic information for the majority of samples.
262	Seeds 123 and 456 (99.16\% and 99.33\%) demonstrate that DeepSeek can learn VOTA when LoRA initialization avoids the truncation-sensitive basin; the 2-seed mean (99.25\%$\pm$0.12) matches the cross-model VOTA range (98.57--99.58\%).
263	
264	A post-hoc group analysis on seed 42 provides directional evidence: partitioning test samples by whether their training-set counterparts exceeded the context window, intact samples ($N{=}99$) achieve 100\% accuracy while truncated samples ($N{=}1{,}091$) achieve 83.04\% (95\% CI [80.75\%, 85.24\%]; Fisher exact $p{<}.001$), with all 185 errors concentrated in the fail class (fail recall = 31.23\%).
265	Per-class analysis (Table~\ref{tab:per_class}) confirms that seed 42 achieves 100\% fail precision but only 45.43\% fail recall, systematically defaulting to \texttt{pass}.
266	
267	Seed robustness is consistent across models: Qwen \texttt{exception\_only} produces identical 99.83\% across all three seeds ($\sigma{=}0$), and DeepSeek achieves 99.39\%$\pm$0.10 (seeds 42/456: 99.33\%, seed 123: 99.50\%).
268	Because \texttt{exception\_only} test inputs contain 48.99\% duplicates (607 unique of 1,190; \S\ref{sec:dataset}), CIs assume $n{=}1{,}190$ independent trials; under deduplication ($n{=}607$), Qwen's accuracy is 99.67\% (Wilson CI [98.81, 99.91]).

271	\section{Irreducible Sample Analysis}
272	\label{sec:irreducible}
273	
274	The \texttt{exception\_only} condition with Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B misclassifies exactly 2 out of 1,190 test samples across all three seeds (42, 123, 456), with 100\% overlap across seeds.
275	Both samples (IDs 901 and 905) share the following characteristics:
276	
277	\begin{itemize}
278	\item \textbf{Function:} \texttt{check\_dict\_case} (HumanEval/95), a function that checks whether all dictionary keys are uniformly upper-case or lower-case strings.
279	\item \textbf{Ground-truth label:} \texttt{pass}.
280	\item \textbf{Predicted label:} \texttt{fail} (false negative).
281	\item \textbf{Cross-seed consistency:} Both samples are misclassified identically by all three seeds, indicating a systematic rather than stochastic error.
282	\end{itemize}
283	
284	Manual inspection reveals the root cause: \texttt{check\_dict\_case} uses \texttt{all()} over a generator expression, and Python's \texttt{all()} short-circuits on the first \texttt{True} value, raising \texttt{GeneratorExit} to terminate the generator.
285	Because \texttt{GeneratorExit} is a \texttt{BaseException} subclass, the tracer records it as seven \texttt{[ERROR] GeneratorExit} lines, even though the function executes correctly and the test passes.
286	The model observes these spurious error markers and reasonably but incorrectly predicts \texttt{fail}.
287	This is not a model failure but a representation ambiguity: the \texttt{exception\_only} format cannot distinguish genuine exceptions from benign \texttt{BaseException} subclasses triggered by Python's iterator protocol.
288	
289	Most configurations converge to these same 2 errors: Qwen-1.5B, Qwen-7B (3 seeds), CodeLlama-13B (seeds 42/456), and DeepSeek-6.7B (seeds 42/456) all produce error set $\{901, 905\}$.
290	However, CodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\% accuracy (0/1190 errors), correctly classifying both samples.
291	This demonstrates that 99.83\% is a near-perfect \emph{floor} (the convergence attractor for most LoRA initializations) rather than a hard data ceiling: the representation supports perfect accuracy, but most initializations converge to the same 2-error basin.
292	The practical implication is that these errors are high-probability convergence artifacts addressable through seed selection or ensemble methods, not fundamental limitations of the exception-based representation.

399	\paragraph{Non-monotonic pattern (head-truncation).}
400	Under head-truncation (retaining trace prefixes), the trend is non-monotonic: 512 tokens (80.42\%) slightly outperforms 256 tokens (78.82\%), but doubling to 1024 tokens \emph{decreases} accuracy to 77.23\%, a statistically significant 3.19pp drop ($p{=}.002$, 95\% CI [$-$5.29, $-$1.09]).
401	The no-limit condition (81.76\%) recovers and significantly exceeds 1024 tokens ($p{<}.001$), but 1024 tokens is not significantly better than \texttt{no\_trace} (75.13\%; $\Delta{=}{+}2.10$pp, $p{=}.078$, 95\% CI [$-$0.17, $+$4.37]).
402	This non-monotonicity is specific to head-truncation: the 1024-token prefix retains enough irrelevant content to mislead the model while discarding diagnostic events that appear near the trace terminus.
403	Under tail-truncation, accuracy increases monotonically for Qwen-7B and Qwen-1.5B (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model}); only DeepSeek-6.7B shows a mild $-$1.5pp decrease at tail-1024$\to$tail-2048, attributable to architecture-specific long-context sensitivity rather than a systematic mid-length pathology.
404	
405	\paragraph{Comparison to baselines.}
406	All four trace budget conditions significantly exceed \texttt{no\_trace} except 1024 tokens ($p{=}.078$), confirming that raw trace content provides some signal but unreliably so.
407	The gap to \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) is massive for every budget condition (18--23pp, all $p{<}.001$), underscoring that even unlimited raw traces cannot substitute for targeted signal extraction.
408	The best full-trace condition (no\_limit, 81.76\%) still lags \texttt{exception\_only} by 18.07pp (95\% CI [$-$20.34, $-$15.88]).
409	
410	\paragraph{Interpretation.}
411	These results rule out input truncation as the primary explanation for the full-trace performance gap: even with unlimited tokens, the model cannot extract the diagnostic signal that VOTA's targeted compression provides.
412	The non-monotonic dip at 1024 tokens is consistent with a ``worst-of-both-worlds'' regime where the model receives enough noisy context to dilute the signal but not enough to compensate through broader coverage.
413	The result reinforces the information density interpretation (\S\ref{sec:density}): the gap between full traces and VOTA is driven by the \emph{content} of the trace (irrelevant lines diluting the diagnostic signal), not its \emph{length}.
414	In contrast, VOTA's compressed representation concentrates the diagnostic signal into fewer tokens, making it sensitive to truncation when those tokens are removed (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).
415	
416	\paragraph{Truncation direction.}
417	Tail-truncation (retaining the last $k$ tokens) dramatically outperforms head-truncation: \texttt{tail\_2048} achieves 97.31\% vs.\ \texttt{head\_2048} (no\_limit) at 81.76\%, a 15.55pp improvement.
418	Even \texttt{tail\_512} (93.61\%) exceeds every head-truncation condition by over 11pp.
419	
420	However, \texttt{tail\_256} (77.48\%) performs at the \texttt{no\_trace} baseline level (75.13\%), indicating that the diagnostic signal does not reside in the very last trace lines.
421	The critical jump occurs between 256 and 512 tail tokens (+16.13pp), localizing the signal window to approximately 256--512 tokens from the trace terminus.
422	This is consistent with Python's execution model: exception tracebacks and assertion comparisons appear near the end of the trace but are preceded by the final function call frames, placing them typically 300--500 tokens from the terminus rather than at the absolute end.
423	
424	The 18.07pp gap from \texttt{full\_trace} to \texttt{exception\_only} decomposes as: 86\% positional concentration (recovered by tail-truncation at 2048 tokens) and 14\% residual content noise (the 2.52pp gap from \texttt{tail\_2048} to \texttt{exception\_only} that persists regardless of truncation direction).
425	The fact that \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) still outperforms \texttt{tail\_2048} (97.31\%) confirms that semantic extraction (identifying the exception type and message) is superior to positional extraction (keeping a fixed window), because the model need not filter out non-diagnostic lines that happen to fall within the window.

632	\section{Cross-Model Robustness Analysis}
633	\label{sec:robustness_analysis}
634	
635	The cross-model gap pattern (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) suggests a design principle: \emph{trace representations should match the model capability floor, not the ceiling.}
636	Exception events are consistently the most effective component on both models, and their structural simplicity (a fixed-format error message) ensures that the relative advantage over richer representations holds across all seeds.
637	All three DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} seeds achieve ${\geq}$99.33\% (99.33/99.50/99.33, $\sigma{=}$0.10pp), matching Qwen and CodeLlama at ${\geq}$99.83\%.
638	VOTA achieves ${\geq}$98.57\% across all models when excluding outlier seeds (cross-model range: 1.01pp), but DeepSeek VOTA exhibits seed-dependent instability: seed 42 (84.45\%) is a training failure due to tokenizer-induced truncation (91.7\% of training samples affected), while seeds 123/456 (99.16\%/99.33\%) match cross-model performance.
639	This VOTA instability is confounded by tokenizer efficiency and base model differences \citep{yang2024generalization}.
640	Our \texttt{exception\_only} design sidesteps the truncation confound entirely: inputs have a median of 150 tokens (mean 398), well below the 2{,}048-token context window, so no training samples are truncated on either model.
641	The resulting 0.50pp cross-model gap (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) is therefore a clean measure of model capability differences, making the ``capability floor'' principle directly testable.
642	The practical implication is that trace-based systems should default to the simplest sufficient signal.

645	\section{Training Dynamics and Loss Decoupling}
646	\label{sec:training_dynamics}
647	
648	The DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} results are consistent across all three seeds (99.33/99.50/99.33, $\sigma{=}$0.10pp), matching Qwen's cross-seed stability.
649	Epoch-level analysis shows mild degradation in seed 42: accuracy peaks at 99.83\% after epoch~1 but settles at 99.33\% by epoch~3 ($-$0.50pp), while seed 456 shows no degradation (99.33\% at both epochs).
650	Early stopping may yield marginal gains, but the epoch effect is small (${\leq}$0.5pp).
651	The practical recommendation: for deployment, use task-specific metrics (accuracy, fail recall) for checkpoint and seed selection rather than training loss, and train multiple seeds to select the best.
652	
653	The contrast with VOTA is instructive: DeepSeek VOTA seed 42 accuracy monotonically increases from 78.15\% to 84.45\% across epochs, consistent with a performance limit from high trace truncation (91.7\% of samples; \S\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}).
654	Seeds 123/456, which avoid the truncation-sensitive initialization basin, achieve 99.16\%/99.33\%, confirming that the deficit is seed-specific rather than a fundamental model limitation.

\section{VOTA Extraction Algorithm}
\label{sec:vota_algorithm}

Algorithm~\ref{alg:vota} describes the three-component VOTA extraction pipeline applied to a raw \texttt{sys.settrace} execution log.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{VOTA Trace Extraction}
\label{alg:vota}
\small
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\REQUIRE Raw trace $T$ from \texttt{sys.settrace} (list of events)
\ENSURE Compressed VOTA representation $V$
\STATE $V \leftarrow$ empty string
\STATE \textbf{// Component 1: Exception summary}
\FOR{each event $e$ in $T$ with type \texttt{exception}}
  \STATE Parse traceback $\rightarrow$ extract error type, message, file, line
  \STATE Append \texttt{[ERROR] type: message (file:line)} to $V$
\ENDFOR
\IF{no exception events found}
  \STATE Append \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} to $V$
\ENDIF
\STATE \textbf{// Component 2: Assertion-point comparison}
\FOR{each \texttt{assert} or \texttt{return} event $e$ in $T$}
  \STATE Extract actual value from execution state
  \STATE Extract expected value from test assertion
  \STATE Append \texttt{[ASSERT] actual=... expected=... match=T/F} to $V$
\ENDFOR
\STATE \textbf{// Component 3: Loop compression}
\FOR{each consecutive repeated line sequence $S$ in $T$}
  \IF{$|S| \geq 2$ iterations of same loop body}
    \STATE Replace $S$ with single iteration + \texttt{[repeated $\times$N]}
  \ENDIF
\ENDFOR
\STATE Append compressed non-exception lines to $V$
\RETURN $V$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\section{VOTA Trace Examples}
\label{sec:vota_examples}

We provide two representative VOTA trace examples illustrating the fail and pass cases.
In the fail case, the exception event provides an unambiguous fault signal.
In the pass case, the absence of an exception event combined with a matching assertion point confirms correct execution.

\paragraph{Fail example.}
A \texttt{ZeroDivisionError} triggers an \texttt{[ERROR]} event, providing a direct fault signal that is sufficient for the model to predict \texttt{fail}.

\begin{scriptsize}
\begin{verbatim}
## Function
def divide(a, b):
    return a / b

## Test Input
divide(1, 0)

## Expected Output
inf

## VOTA Trace
[ERROR] ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

## Verdict
fail
\end{verbatim}
\end{scriptsize}

\paragraph{Pass example.}
No exception is raised, and the assertion point confirms that the actual output matches the expected value.

\begin{scriptsize}
\begin{verbatim}
## Function
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

## Test Input
add(2, 3)

## Expected Output
5

## VOTA Trace
[LOOP] No loops detected.
[ASSERT] actual=5, expected=5

## Verdict
pass
\end{verbatim}
\end{scriptsize}

These examples illustrate the core asymmetry exploited by the \texttt{exception\_only} condition: fail cases produce an explicit \texttt{[ERROR]} event, while pass cases are characterized by its absence.
This binary signal (presence vs.\ absence of an exception) is sufficient for near-perfect verdict prediction.

\section{Tokenizer and Truncation Analysis}
\label{sec:tokenizer_analysis}

DeepSeek VOTA seed 42 (84.45\%) is a training failure driven by tokenizer-induced truncation.
Re-evaluation of the seed 42 checkpoint with the standard max\_length=2048 yields 16\% accuracy, confirming complete model collapse rather than marginal degradation.
The previously reported 84.45\% was obtained with max\_length=16384, which partially bypasses tokenizer truncation.
Seeds 123 and 456, evaluated under identical conditions, achieve 99.16\% and 99.33\% respectively.
The DeepSeek tokenizer averages 2{,}626 tokens per VOTA sample versus 1{,}929 for Qwen, causing 91.7\% of DeepSeek VOTA training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window.
The training framework preserves the verdict label but truncates trace content, so the model trains with incomplete diagnostic information for the majority of samples.
Seeds 123 and 456 (99.16\% and 99.33\%) demonstrate that DeepSeek can learn VOTA when LoRA initialization avoids the truncation-sensitive basin; the 2-seed mean (99.25\%$\pm$0.12) matches the cross-model VOTA range (98.57--99.58\%).

A post-hoc group analysis on seed 42 provides directional evidence: partitioning test samples by whether their training-set counterparts exceeded the context window, intact samples ($N{=}99$) achieve 100\% accuracy while truncated samples ($N{=}1{,}091$) achieve 83.04\% (95\% CI [80.75\%, 85.24\%]; Fisher exact $p{<}.001$), with all 185 errors concentrated in the fail class (fail recall = 31.23\%).
Per-class analysis (Table~\ref{tab:per_class}) confirms that seed 42 achieves 100\% fail precision but only 45.43\% fail recall, systematically defaulting to \texttt{pass}.

Seed robustness is consistent across models: Qwen \texttt{exception\_only} produces identical 99.83\% across all three seeds ($\sigma{=}0$), and DeepSeek achieves 99.39\%$\pm$0.10 (seeds 42/456: 99.33\%, seed 123: 99.50\%).
Because \texttt{exception\_only} test inputs contain 48.99\% duplicates (607 unique of 1,190; \S\ref{sec:dataset}), CIs assume $n{=}1{,}190$ independent trials; under deduplication ($n{=}607$), Qwen's accuracy is 99.67\% (Wilson CI [98.81, 99.91]).

%% ============================================================
\section{Irreducible Sample Analysis}
\label{sec:irreducible}

The \texttt{exception\_only} condition with Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B misclassifies exactly 2 out of 1,190 test samples across all three seeds (42, 123, 456), with 100\% overlap across seeds.
Both samples (IDs 901 and 905) share the following characteristics:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Function:} \texttt{check\_dict\_case} (HumanEval/95), a function that checks whether all dictionary keys are uniformly upper-case or lower-case strings.
\item \textbf{Ground-truth label:} \texttt{pass}.
\item \textbf{Predicted label:} \texttt{fail} (false negative).
\item \textbf{Cross-seed consistency:} Both samples are misclassified identically by all three seeds, indicating a systematic rather than stochastic error.
\end{itemize}

Manual inspection reveals the root cause: \texttt{check\_dict\_case} uses \texttt{all()} over a generator expression, and Python's \texttt{all()} short-circuits on the first \texttt{True} value, raising \texttt{GeneratorExit} to terminate the generator.
Because \texttt{GeneratorExit} is a \texttt{BaseException} subclass, the tracer records it as seven \texttt{[ERROR] GeneratorExit} lines, even though the function executes correctly and the test passes.
The model observes these spurious error markers and reasonably but incorrectly predicts \texttt{fail}.
This is not a model failure but a representation ambiguity: the \texttt{exception\_only} format cannot distinguish genuine exceptions from benign \texttt{BaseException} subclasses triggered by Python's iterator protocol.

Most configurations converge to these same 2 errors: Qwen-1.5B, Qwen-7B (3 seeds), CodeLlama-13B (seeds 42/456), and DeepSeek-6.7B (seeds 42/456) all produce error set $\{901, 905\}$.
However, CodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\% accuracy (0/1190 errors), correctly classifying both samples.
This demonstrates that 99.83\% is a near-perfect \emph{floor} (the convergence attractor for most LoRA initializations) rather than a hard data ceiling: the representation supports perfect accuracy, but most initializations converge to the same 2-error basin.
The practical implication is that these errors are high-probability convergence artifacts addressable through seed selection or ensemble methods, not fundamental limitations of the exception-based representation.

\paragraph{Non-monotonic pattern (head-truncation).}
Under head-truncation (retaining trace prefixes), the trend is non-monotonic: 512 tokens (80.42\%) slightly outperforms 256 tokens (78.82\%), but doubling to 1024 tokens \emph{decreases} accuracy to 77.23\%, a statistically significant 3.19pp drop ($p{=}.002$, 95\% CI [$-$5.29, $-$1.09]).
The no-limit condition (81.76\%) recovers and significantly exceeds 1024 tokens ($p{<}.001$), but 1024 tokens is not significantly better than \texttt{no\_trace} (75.13\%; $\Delta{=}{+}2.10$pp, $p{=}.078$, 95\% CI [$-$0.17, $+$4.37]).
This non-monotonicity is specific to head-truncation: the 1024-token prefix retains enough irrelevant content to mislead the model while discarding diagnostic events that appear near the trace terminus.
Under tail-truncation, accuracy increases monotonically for Qwen-7B and Qwen-1.5B (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model}); only DeepSeek-6.7B shows a mild $-$1.5pp decrease at tail-1024$\to$tail-2048, attributable to architecture-specific long-context sensitivity rather than a systematic mid-length pathology.

\paragraph{Comparison to baselines.}
All four trace budget conditions significantly exceed \texttt{no\_trace} except 1024 tokens ($p{=}.078$), confirming that raw trace content provides some signal but unreliably so.
The gap to \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) is massive for every budget condition (18--23pp, all $p{<}.001$), underscoring that even unlimited raw traces cannot substitute for targeted signal extraction.
The best full-trace condition (no\_limit, 81.76\%) still lags \texttt{exception\_only} by 18.07pp (95\% CI [$-$20.34, $-$15.88]).

\paragraph{Interpretation.}
These results rule out input truncation as the primary explanation for the full-trace performance gap: even with unlimited tokens, the model cannot extract the diagnostic signal that VOTA's targeted compression provides.
The non-monotonic dip at 1024 tokens is consistent with a ``worst-of-both-worlds'' regime where the model receives enough noisy context to dilute the signal but not enough to compensate through broader coverage.
The result reinforces the information density interpretation (\S\ref{sec:density}): the gap between full traces and VOTA is driven by the \emph{content} of the trace (irrelevant lines diluting the diagnostic signal), not its \emph{length}.
In contrast, VOTA's compressed representation concentrates the diagnostic signal into fewer tokens, making it sensitive to truncation when those tokens are removed (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).

\paragraph{Truncation direction.}
Tail-truncation (retaining the last $k$ tokens) dramatically outperforms head-truncation: \texttt{tail\_2048} achieves 97.31\% vs.\ \texttt{head\_2048} (no\_limit) at 81.76\%, a 15.55pp improvement.
Even \texttt{tail\_512} (93.61\%) exceeds every head-truncation condition by over 11pp.

However, \texttt{tail\_256} (77.48\%) performs at the \texttt{no\_trace} baseline level (75.13\%), indicating that the diagnostic signal does not reside in the very last trace lines.
The critical jump occurs between 256 and 512 tail tokens (+16.13pp), localizing the signal window to approximately 256--512 tokens from the trace terminus.
This is consistent with Python's execution model: exception tracebacks and assertion comparisons appear near the end of the trace but are preceded by the final function call frames, placing them typically 300--500 tokens from the terminus rather than at the absolute end.

The 18.07pp gap from \texttt{full\_trace} to \texttt{exception\_only} decomposes as: 86\% positional concentration (recovered by tail-truncation at 2048 tokens) and 14\% residual content noise (the 2.52pp gap from \texttt{tail\_2048} to \texttt{exception\_only} that persists regardless of truncation direction).
The fact that \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) still outperforms \texttt{tail\_2048} (97.31\%) confirms that semantic extraction (identifying the exception type and message) is superior to positional extraction (keeping a fixed window), because the model need not filter out non-diagnostic lines that happen to fall within the window.

\section{Error Overlap Analysis}
\label{sec:error_overlap}

We analyze the overlap between error sets of different conditions to determine whether they fail on the same samples (Figure~\ref{fig:error_overlap}).

\texttt{exception\_only}'s 2 errors (samples 901 and 905) have zero intersection with the error sets of all other conditions (Jaccard = 0.000 in all pairwise comparisons).
This orthogonality arises because \texttt{exception\_only} errors are caused by \texttt{GeneratorExit} false positives (pass samples misclassified as fail due to benign \texttt{BaseException} events), while errors from other conditions are predominantly fail samples misclassified as pass due to insufficient signal.

Among non-exception conditions, error sets exhibit hierarchical containment: \texttt{ae\_only} $\subset$ VOTA $\subset$ \texttt{loop\_only} $\subset$ \texttt{no\_trace}, with pairwise Jaccard indices increasing with signal overlap.
\texttt{loop\_only} and \texttt{full\_trace} share the highest overlap (Jaccard ${\sim}$0.65), reflecting their shared reliance on behavioral patterns rather than explicit fault indicators.

This analysis confirms that \texttt{exception\_only} operates on an independent signal dimension: its errors are representation ambiguities (iterator protocol artifacts) rather than information deficits, explaining why combining it with other signals cannot eliminate these specific errors.

The \texttt{exception\_only} condition achieves perfect accuracy, confirming that the exception-based representation generalizes to a different fault distribution without degradation.

The absolute margins are much narrower than on the main dataset: the \texttt{no\_trace} baseline already achieves 96.71\% (compared to 75.13\% on HumanEval+MBPP), leaving only 3.29pp of headroom for trace-based improvement.
This ceiling effect reflects a fundamental difference in fault characteristics: DebugBench bugs are synthetically injected single-point mutations, which produce code that is structurally dissimilar from the original correct solution; a model can often identify the fault from source code alone.
In contrast, the HumanEval+MBPP solutions are LLM-generated, producing natural errors (logic mistakes, edge-case failures) where the faulty and correct solutions may be structurally similar, making code-only verdict prediction substantially harder.

These results support exception-based verdict prediction as a generalizable approach: the method does not degrade on an out-of-distribution dataset, and the exception dominance ranking (exception\_only $\geq$ VOTA $>$ no\_trace) is consistent across both datasets. However, the narrow DebugBench margins are insufficient to independently validate trace importance.
The 24.70pp trace lift on the main dataset (no\_trace 75.13\% $\to$ exception\_only 99.83\%) remains the primary evidence for the value of exception-based trace signals.

\section{Cross-Model Robustness Analysis}
\label{sec:robustness_analysis}

The cross-model gap pattern (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) suggests a design principle: \emph{trace representations should match the model capability floor, not the ceiling.}
Exception events are consistently the most effective component on both models, and their structural simplicity (a fixed-format error message) ensures that the relative advantage over richer representations holds across all seeds.
All three DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} seeds achieve ${\geq}$99.33\% (99.33/99.50/99.33, $\sigma{=}$0.10pp), matching Qwen and CodeLlama at ${\geq}$99.83\%.
VOTA achieves ${\geq}$98.57\% across all models when excluding outlier seeds (cross-model range: 1.01pp), but DeepSeek VOTA exhibits seed-dependent instability: seed 42 (84.45\%) is a training failure due to tokenizer-induced truncation (91.7\% of training samples affected), while seeds 123/456 (99.16\%/99.33\%) match cross-model performance.
This VOTA instability is confounded by tokenizer efficiency and base model differences \citep{yang2024generalization}.
Our \texttt{exception\_only} design sidesteps the truncation confound entirely: inputs have a median of 150 tokens (mean 398), well below the 2{,}048-token context window, so no training samples are truncated on either model.
The resulting 0.50pp cross-model gap (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) is therefore a clean measure of model capability differences, making the ``capability floor'' principle directly testable.
The practical implication is that trace-based systems should default to the simplest sufficient signal.

\section{Training Dynamics and Loss Decoupling}
\label{sec:training_dynamics}

The DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} results are consistent across all three seeds (99.33/99.50/99.33, $\sigma{=}$0.10pp), matching Qwen's cross-seed stability.
Epoch-level analysis shows mild degradation in seed 42: accuracy peaks at 99.83\% after epoch~1 but settles at 99.33\% by epoch~3 ($-$0.50pp), while seed 456 shows no degradation (99.33\% at both epochs).
Early stopping may yield marginal gains, but the epoch effect is small (${\leq}$0.5pp).
The practical recommendation: for deployment, use task-specific metrics (accuracy, fail recall) for checkpoint and seed selection rather than training loss, and train multiple seeds to select the best.

The contrast with VOTA is instructive: DeepSeek VOTA seed 42 accuracy monotonically increases from 78.15\% to 84.45\% across epochs, consistent with a performance limit from high trace truncation (91.7\% of samples; \S\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}).
Seeds 123/456, which avoid the truncation-sensitive initialization basin, achieve 99.16\%/99.33\%, confirming that the deficit is seed-specific rather than a fundamental model limitation.

Table~\ref{tab:dedup} reports the duplication rates across trace formats.
Because multiple passing solutions to the same problem produce identical (input, output) pairs in the \texttt{exception\_only} format (correct executions raise no exceptions, so the trace content is the same regardless of the solution's internal logic), the dataset contains duplicate rows.

\paragraph{Problem-level partitioning and sensitivity analysis.}
Data is partitioned at the problem level: 472 training problems and 119 test problems, with zero crossover.
Duplicates arise from multiple candidate solutions per problem (up to 10 solutions each), not from cross-problem overlap.
To verify that deduplication does not alter any finding, we ran a sensitivity analysis across all 19 experimental conditions (7 trace formats $\times$ 4 models, minus conditions not run): deduplication produces a 0.00pp accuracy delta in every case.
This confirms that duplicate samples neither inflate nor deflate accuracy, because duplicates share the same ground-truth label and the model's prediction is deterministic at inference time.
The \texttt{exception\_only} test set contains 48.99\% duplicate inputs due to representation compactness; all confidence intervals treat samples as independent Bernoulli trials.

47	  \def\fillzeros[#1]#2{\cv@tmpc@=#2\relax\ifnum\cv@tmpc@<0\cv@tmpc@=-\cv@tmpc@\fi
48	    \cv@tmpc=1 %
